newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu revamps Zaire's army command.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu revamps Zaire's army command.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, his armed forces struggling to contain rebel thrusts from the east, has shaken up the army high command, naming a new commander of land forces.
State radio reported on Saturday that Mobutu, currently at his villa in the south of France, had named General Mosala Modjandongo, commander of the Lower Zaire region, to the post.
The radio said that Mosala had replaced General Mulumba Ambote as one of the most senior officers in the chaotic Central African nation's notoriously ill-disciplined army.
It quoted a presidential decree signed by Mobutu on February 17, before his departure for France on Friday.
The shake-up follows advances by rebels from the east on several fronts blunting an army counter-offensive launched from Zaire's third city of Kisangani on January 20.

Defence officials contacted by Reuters on Saturday were unable to elaborate on the reasons for the latest change in the high command since the mainly Tutsi-led rebels took up arms last October and seized towns and territory in the east.
Mobutu, who had prostate surgery last August in Europe, returned to Zaire in December after four months' convalesence and shuffled the army high command.

He appointed General Mahele Lieko Bokungo as armed forces chief of staff. Mahele is one of the few senior generals in Zaire who has earned his reputation on the battlefield and not through close family or ethnic ties to Mobutu.

Since then, the army has had new arms and equipment but has failed so far to dent the rebel hold on the east. The government accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the rebels, a charge all three deny.
A senior Defence Ministry official said earlier on Saturday that Zaire's armed forces had been using helicopter gunships to attack rebels advancing from the north and east on Kisangani.

"Since Wednesday our MI-24 combat helicopter have been conducting raids between Bafwasende and Banalia," the official told Reuters, adding that rebels had been as close as 130 km (80 miles) to the city. The raids continued on Friday.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has named Kisangani, strategically placed on the Zaire River, as a target.

Kabila had set a deadline of February 21 for launching an all-out rebel offensive unless Kinshasa agreed to negotiate but following peace moves in South Africa last week, he delayed the planned offensive as a goodwill gesture.
"We're willing to sustain this goodwill for a few days," he said.

But aid workers said 30,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees abandoned their camp at Kalima, up to 400 km (250 miles) south of Kisangani, on Saturday because of fighting and disappeared into the surrounding rain forest.

The U.N. refugee agency said on Saturday that more than 200,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees were unaccounted for in east Zaire since being uprooted by fighting. An estimated 193,000 have been located in the war zone.
Mobutu returned to France for three weeks last month for medical tests. This time, he was expected to stay four days.
